title: Training Webpage Template: User Guide
text:
Welcome to the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template User Guide!
The SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template helps training organisers across SciLifeLab create consistent, reusable and FAIR training websites. No programming is needed: you fill in text files with information about your training, write your materials in Markdown, and the website is built and published for you.

How a training website is organised
Each training gets one website with two main parts:

A landing page with general information about the training and links to every time it is given.
A training instance for each time the training is given, with its own overview, schedule, materials and practical information.



What this guide covers
This guide takes you step by step from an empty template to a published, citable training website. It covers how to:

create your own copy of the template and preview it on your computer;
set up the landing page;
create a training instance and add your materials;
prepare your training materials for publication, citation, and reuse following FAIR principles.

No prior experience with Git, Python or Quarto is needed. Start with Set up your training and follow it once from beginning to end. After that, you can go straight to the chapter you need.



This User Guide is maintained by the SciLifeLab Training Hub.
Questions, problems or ideas for improving the guide or the template? Open an issue or email us at training@scilifelab.se.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.1 Install the software
This chapter takes you through everything you need to do once, at the start, to get your own training website. You will create your own copy of the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template, publish it as a website, and set it up on your computer so you can edit it.
This is the only part of the guide you do just once, and takes about an hour. Take your time: each step explains what you are doing and why, and what you should see when it worked.
Once you are done, the next chapter, Regular workflow, shows the few steps you repeat every time you update your website.
To work with the template, you need a free GitHub account and four free programs. If you already have some of them, you can skip those.
Install each program with the default settings. Then open Visual Studio Code (VS Code) once, to check that it starts.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.2 Create your repository
A repository is the folder on GitHub that holds everything for your training: the information about it, the materials, and the website. You create your own repository as a copy of the template. The template itself stays unchanged, so you can’t break anything for others.

Open the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template on GitHub.
In the top-right corner of the page, click the green Use this template button and select Create a new repository.



Fill in the form:

Turn Include all branches on. This is required: the template keeps the landing page and each training instance in separate branches (you will learn about these later), and you need all of them.
Under Owner, select the GitHub organisation or account where the repository should live, for example SciLifeLab-Training, NBISweden, or your personal account.
Under Repository name, enter a short name in lowercase, with hyphens instead of spaces, for example introduction-to-r. The name becomes part of your website address, so choose it carefully.
Under Visibility, choose Public, so participants can see the website and materials.

Click Create repository.


GitHub now opens your new repository. Check the name at the top of the page: it should be the name you just chose, not the template’s name.







TipWorking with others? Add collaborators (optional)





If other people will help develop or maintain the training, give them access to the repository. You can also do this later.

In your repository, click Settings. 
Under Access in the menu on the left, click Collaborators and teams. 
Click Add people or Add teams.
Search for the person or team, choose a role, and click Add. 

The options you see depend on whether the repository belongs to you or to an organisation, and on your permissions in that organisation.




Done when: you see your own repository on GitHub, with the name you chose.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.3 Publish your website
Your new repository already contains a ready-made copy of the template website, and GitHub usually publishes it and sets it up by itself. In this step you check two settings, and add your website link to your repository’s main page.

Check that your website is online

In your repository, click Settings, then Pages in the menu on the left. 
At the top of the page, look for Your site is live at, followed by your website address. It looks like https://ORGANISATION.github.io/REPOSITORY-NAME/, with your organisation (or user name) and repository name filled in. 

For now, your website shows the template’s example content. It changes to your own content the first time you upload a change.






NoteDon’t see “Your site is live at”?





Sometimes GitHub doesn’t switch on publishing by itself. You can do it yourself:

On the same page, under Source, choose Deploy from a branch.
Under Branch, choose gh-pages and / (root), and click Save. 
Wait a minute or two and refresh the page. Your site is live at now appears at the top.






Check that your website can be updated
Every time you upload a change, GitHub runs a small automatic process that rebuilds your website. This process needs permission to update the website.

Click Settings, then Actions → General in the menu on the left.
Scroll down to Workflow permissions, and check that Read and write permissions is selected. 







NoteIs “Read repository contents and packages permissions” selected instead?





Select Read and write permissions and click Save.
If you can’t select it because the option is greyed out, your organisation controls this setting. Ask an administrator of the organisation to allow it for your repository.





Add the website link to your repository
Show the website address on your repository’s main page, so you can always find your website quickly:

Click the Code tab to go back to the repository’s main page. 
On the right-hand side, next to About, click the gear icon ⚙️.
Tick Use your GitHub Pages website and click Save changes. 


Done when: the website link appears under About, and clicking it opens the template website.

title: 2  Set up your training
section: 2.4 Open the repository on your computer
text:
2.4 Open the repository on your computer
So far, your repository only exists on GitHub. To edit it, you make a copy on your computer. This is called cloning.
Working on a copy has a big advantage: nothing you change is visible to anyone else until you decide to upload it. You can try things out, look at the result, and undo mistakes, all safely on your own computer.

On your repository’s main page on GitHub, click the green Code button, make sure HTTPS is selected, and copy the address.

Open VS Code and click Clone Git Repository on the start screen. If you don’t see it, open View → Command Palette, type Git: Clone and press Enter.

Paste the HTTPS address you copied and press Enter.
Choose where to save the repository on your computer, for example a folder called GitHub inside Documents, and click Select as Repository Destination. 
When VS Code asks whether to open the repository, click Open.

The files and folders of your repository now appear in the Explorer panel on the left side of VS Code. Throughout this guide, you open files by clicking them there.
If VS Code suggests installing recommended extensions, click Install. They help VS Code understand the files used in the template.







TipPrefer the terminal?





cd ~/Documents/GitHub
git clone https://github.com/ORGANISATION/REPOSITORY-NAME.git
Then open the new folder in VS Code with File → Open Folder…




✓ Done when: you see your repository’s files in the Explorer panel in VS Code.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.5 Set up the environment
Your website is built by a few small Python scripts that come with the template. These scripts need one extra Python package. In this step you install it in a separate, self-contained environment inside your repository folder, so it doesn’t interfere with anything else on your computer.
You only do this once for each repository. You don’t need to understand the commands: copy each one exactly as shown.

Open a terminal
A terminal is a window where you type commands. In VS Code, choose Terminal → New Terminal.

The terminal opens at the bottom of the window, already inside your repository folder.
To run a command from this guide, copy it, paste it into the terminal, and press Enter.



Check the software
First, check that Git, Python and Quarto were installed correctly. Run these commands one by one:

macOS and LinuxWindows


git --version
python3 --version
quarto --version


git --version
python --version
quarto --version



Each command should print a version number, for example Python 3.12.4 (see image above). If one says command not found, install that program again, restart VS Code, and try again.


Create the environment
Run these three commands one by one. The last one can take a minute.

macOS and LinuxWindows


python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt


python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt



The first command creates the environment, the second switches it on, and the third installs what the scripts need. When the environment is switched on, the terminal line starts with (.venv):
(.venv) username@computer introduction-to-r %



Let VS Code switch on the environment
The environment has to be switched on each time you open a new terminal. You can let VS Code do that for you:

Press Cmd+Shift+P (macOS) or Ctrl+Shift+P (Windows and Linux).
Type Python: Select Interpreter and press Enter.
Choose the option that shows .venv.


From now on, every new terminal you open in this repository starts with the environment switched on.

Done when: a new terminal (Terminal → New Terminal) starts with (.venv).

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
You’re all set!
Your training has its own repository and website, and your computer is ready to edit it. You won’t need to repeat any of these steps for this training.
Continue with Regular workflow to make your first change and see it appear on your website.



This User Guide is maintained by the SciLifeLab Training Hub.
Questions, problems or ideas for improving the guide or the template? Open an issue or email us at training@scilifelab.se.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.1 Open your training
This chapter shows the steps you repeat every time you work on your training website: open your training, preview it, make your changes, and publish them.
The steps are always the same, whether you change a date, add a team member or write a new page of materials. The cheat sheet at the end of this chapter lists all of them on one screen, for when you just need a reminder.
Each time you start working, open your repository in VS Code and make sure you have the latest version.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
Open VS Code. It usually reopens the repository you worked on last. 
If not, choose File → Open Recent, or File → Open Folder… and select your repository folder.

Get the latest version. If you work together with others, they may have uploaded changes since you last worked. In the bottom-left corner of VS Code, click the circular arrows next to the branch name (Synchronize Changes). This downloads their changes to your computer.



Which part of your website are you working on?
The bottom-left corner of VS Code also shows the branch you are working on. Your repository keeps each part of your training website in its own branch:

main: the training landing page.
release- followed by four digits, for example release-2605: one training instance, here the one in May 2026.


Before you start editing, check that you are on the branch you want to change. For your first change below, stay on main.

Done when: your repository is open in VS Code, and the bottom-left corner shows the branch you want to work on.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.2 Preview your website
A preview shows your website in your web browser while you work on it, before anything is published. The preview runs on your own computer, so only you can see it. This lets you check every change before your collaborators or participants see it.
To start the preview, open a terminal (Terminal → New Terminal, see Open a terminal) and run:
python scripts/preview.py

Quarto now builds your website. After a few seconds, it opens in your web browser.

If it doesn’t open by itself, copy the address shown in the terminal, for example http://localhost:4268/, and paste it into your browser.
Keep the preview running while you work. Each time you save a file (Cmd+S (macOS) or Ctrl+S (Windows and Linux)), the preview updates by itself.

To run other commands while the preview is running, open a second terminal with Terminal → New Terminal. The terminal running the preview is busy.
To stop the preview when you are done, click in the terminal where it runs and press Ctrl+C.







TipAnother way to start the preview: the Preview button





When a page file (ending in .qmd) is open in VS Code, you can also click the Preview button in the top-right corner of the editor.

The website then opens inside VS Code. To see it in your browser instead, click Open in Browser.





Done when: your website is open in your browser.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.3 Make a change
Almost everything on your website comes from the files in the data folder: the title, dates, team, schedule, and so on. You change your website by changing these files, without touching any code.
How these files are organised is explained in Repository structure. For now, we focus on making one change and publishing it, so you can see the whole process from start to finish.
As a first change, try changing the title of your training:

In the Explorer panel, open the data folder and click course.yml.



Scroll down a bit and find the line:
title: "Training title"
Change the text between the quotation marks, for example:
title: "Introduction to R"



Save the file with Cmd+S (macOS) or Ctrl+S (Windows and Linux).

The new title appears at the top of the preview in your browser.







Warning



The data files are sensitive to layout. Keep the quotation marks, and keep the spaces at the start of each line exactly as they are. If the preview shows an error after you save, check those first. The lines starting with # are explanations: they don’t appear on the website.



Done when: the preview shows your new title.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.4 Commit and push your changes
Your change is now saved on your computer, but nobody else can see it yet. Publishing it takes two steps, both in VS Code’s Source Control panel:

Commit: save a version of your changes, with a short description of what you changed. Each commit is kept, so you can always see what changed and when.
Push: upload your commits to GitHub. GitHub then updates your website automatically.


Click the Source Control icon on the left side of VS Code. Your changed files are listed under Changes.
You changed only course.yml, but you probably see more files, for example files in the _generated folder. That’s expected: the template updates these files automatically from your data files, while the preview runs. Depending on what you change, you may also see README.md, CITATION.cff or .zenodo.json. Always commit all changed files together.

Hover over the word Changes and click the + next to it (Stage All Changes). This tells VS Code to include all changed files in your commit. They move to Staged Changes.

In the Message box at the top, describe your change, for example Change the training title.

Click Commit.
Click Sync Changes to push your commit to GitHub.








Note



The first time you push, VS Code may ask you to sign in to GitHub. Follow the instructions in your browser, then return to VS Code.








TipChanged something by mistake?





Before you commit, you can undo all changes to a file: in the Source Control panel, hover over the file and click the curved arrow (Discard Changes). The file goes back to how it was at your last commit.

You only need to do this for the files you changed yourself, such as data/course.yml. The files the template updates automatically, for example in the _generated folder, go back by themselves: as soon as you discard your own change, the preview rebuilds them, and they disappear from the list after a few seconds.
This only works while the preview is running. If they are still listed, start the preview (python scripts/preview.py) and wait a few seconds.




Done when: the Source Control panel shows no more changes.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.5 Check the published website
After you push, GitHub rebuilds and publishes your website by itself. This usually takes one or two minutes. You can follow it on GitHub:

Open your repository on GitHub and click the Actions tab.

Wait until both of these show a green checkmark:

deploy-landing (or deploy-instance, when you changed a training instance): builds your website;
pages build and deployment: publishes it.


A yellow dot means it is still running.
Open your website with the link under About on your repository’s main page, see About link.







Tip



Still seeing the old version? Wait a minute and refresh the page. Browsers sometimes show an older copy for a short while.
A red cross in the Actions tab means something went wrong. Click it to see the error message, or see the cheat sheet below.



Done when: your published website shows your change.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
Next steps
You now know the routine for every change. Continue with:

Repository structure: find your way around your repository, and learn which files to change and which to leave alone.
Landing page: describe your training on the landing page.
Training instances: create the website for each time your training is given.

Questions, problems or ideas for improving the guide or the template? Open an issue or email us at training@scilifelab.se.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
4.1 Branches
You now know the routine for making a change and publishing it, from Regular workflow. You’re ready to make the template your own, with the information and materials of your training.
Before you start, it helps to know how your repository is organised. This chapter shows you where everything lives, so you always know where to make a change, and which files you don’t need to edit.
Your training repository is divided into branches. Each branch holds the files for one part of your website. A new repository made from the template has three branches: main, release-0000 and gh-pages.
Each of these branches holds the files for one part of your website:
Because each training instance has its own branch, you can prepare the next training without changing the website of an earlier one. Participants of earlier trainings can always go back to the materials as they were.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
The main branch holds the landing page: the general page about your training, with its description, learning outcomes and team, and links to every time the training is given.

The gh-pages branch holds the published website: the finished pages that visitors see. GitHub builds them from your other branches and updates this branch automatically every time you push a change.







Warning



Never edit the gh-pages branch yourself. GitHub updates it automatically every time you push a change to one of the other branches.



The release-0000 branch is an example training instance: the website for one time the training is given, with its dates, schedule, practical information, team and training materials. You use it as the starting point for each new training instance, which gets a branch of its own.




Branch names
A training instance branch is named release- followed by the year and month of the training, written as YYMM. For example, release-2705 is the training in May 2027.


An example
This is what the branches look like in a repository for a training that has been given twice, in May 2026 and May 2027:
Your repository
│
├── main              The landing page: the general page about your
│                     training, with links to every training instance.
│
├── release-2605      The website of your training in May 2026.
├── release-2705      The website of your training in May 2027.
│
├── release-0000      The example training instance that comes with
│                     the template.
│
└── gh-pages          The published website. Updated automatically.
In this repository, you would work on these branches:



I want to…
I work on branch…




Change the landing page
main


Edit the materials of the May 2026 training
release-2605


Fix a typo on the May 2027 website
release-2705


Set up the next training instance
A new release- branch: see Training instances









Note



You work on one branch at a time. To learn how to switch to another branch in VS Code, see Switch branch.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
4.2 Three kinds of files
When you open a branch of your repository in VS Code, you see many files and folders. Don’t worry: you only have to work with a few of them. On all branches, the files fall into three groups:








Icon
Kind
What it means for you




✏️
Files you edit
Your information and materials. This is where you make your changes.


🔄
Files that are updated automatically
The template creates and updates these files automatically. You should not edit them, but if you accidentally do, your edits will automatically be overwritten.


🔒
Files you can leave alone
The parts that make the template work, you never need to change these.









Tip



The automatically updated files 🔄 often appear in the Source Control panel when you only changed a data file. That’s expected: commit them together with your own changes, as described in Commit and push your changes.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
4.3 Files on the main branch
On the main branch, everything for your training’s landing page lives in these files and folders:

The table below explains what each one is for, and whether you edit it ✏️, it’s updated automatically 🔄, or you can leave it alone 🔒.








File or folder
What it contains
Kind of file




data/course.yml
The title, description, learning outcomes and keywords of your training, and how others may reuse and cite it
✏️


data/team.yml
The people behind the training
✏️


data/website.yml
The logos, button texts and footer of the landing page
✏️


data/instances.yml
The list of training instances, with links to their websites
✏️


img/
The images and logos used on the landing page
✏️


docs/
The README for your training (_template-README.md), which you copy over README.md when you start, and documentation for developers of the template
✏️ 🔄


README.md
The description shown on your repository’s main page on GitHub. The parts between <!-- generated:... --> lines are updated automatically; you can edit the rest
✏️ 🔄


_generated/
The sections of the landing page, built from your data files
🔄


CITATION.cff
How to cite your training, built from your data files
🔄


.zenodo.json
The information Zenodo uses when you publish your training, built from your data files
🔄


LICENSE.md
The full text of the licence of your training: CC BY 4.0, unless you choose another licence in data/course.yml. Only replace it if you do
✏️🔒


CONTRIBUTING.md
How others can report problems and suggest improvements to your training.Ready to use, but you can adapt it if you like
✏️🔒


index.qmd, _sections/
The building blocks that put the landing page together
🔒


styles.css
The look of the website: colours, fonts and layout
🔒


_template/
Information about the template itself, used only while template mode is on. You can delete it once you’ve switched template mode off
🔒


scripts/, tests/
The scripts that build the website, and the checks that test them
🔒


.github/
The automatic processes that publish your website on GitHub
🔒


.vscode/
Settings for VS Code, such as the extensions it recommends when you open the repository
🔒


.gitignore
The list of files that stay on your computer and are never uploaded to GitHub, such as your preview and environment
🔒


_quarto.yml, requirements.txt, requirements-dev.txt
Settings for Quarto, and the Python packages the scripts need
🔒



When you preview your website, a few more folders appear on your computer: _site/ (the website itself), .quarto/ and .venv/ (your environment). They are listed in .gitignore, so they are never uploaded to GitHub, and you can ignore them.

title: 4  Repository structure
section: 4.4 Files on a training instance branch
text:
4.4 Files on a training instance branch
A training instance branch has the same structure as main, plus the information pages of the specific training instance, your training materials, and (reuse) guidance for training instructors.

The table below explains what each one is for, and whether you edit it ✏️, it’s updated automatically 🔄, or you can leave it alone 🔒.








File or folder
What it contains
Kind of file




data/course.yml
The title, dates, location and description of this training instance, and how others may reuse and cite it (required)
✏️


data/team.yml
The organisers, instructors and helpers (required)
✏️


data/website.yml
The logos, texts and sections of the overview page, and the footer (required)
✏️


data/schedule.yml
The schedule of the training (optional)
✏️


data/announcements.yml, practicalities.yml, preparation.yml, faq.yml, resources.yml
The information pages (optional)
✏️


content/
Your training materials, with one folder per module
✏️


instructors/
Notes for instructors: timing, preparation and teaching notes for each module. Not shown on the website, but anyone can read it on GitHub
✏️


img/
The images, logos and photos used on the website
✏️


README.md
The description shown on your repository’s main page on GitHub. The parts between <!-- generated:... --> lines are updated automatically; you can edit the rest
✏️ 🔄


CONTRIBUTING.md
How others can report problems and suggest improvements to your training. Ready to use, but you can adapt it if you like
✏️🔒


LICENSE.md
The full text of the licence of your training: CC BY 4.0, unless you choose another licence in data/course.yml. Only replace it if you do
✏️🔒


_generated/
The sections of the website, built from your data files
🔄


CITATION.cff, .zenodo.json
How to cite this training instance, and the information Zenodo uses, built from your data files
🔄


index.qmd, schedule.qmd, team.qmd and the other .qmd files
The pages of the website. They collect their content from your data files
🔒


_sections/, js/, styles.css
The building blocks, interactive parts and look of the website
🔒


scripts/, .github/, docs/
The scripts that build the website, the automatic processes that publish it, and documentation for developers of the template
🔒


_quarto.yml, requirements.txt, .gitignore
Settings for Quarto, the Python packages the scripts need, and the list of files that are never uploaded to GitHub
🔒



When you preview your website, a few more folders appear on your computer: _site/ (the website itself), .quarto/ and .venv/ (your environment). They are listed in .gitignore, so they are never uploaded to GitHub, and you can ignore them.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
Data files
As the tables above show, most of the files you edit are data files: the files ending in .yml in the data folder.
When you open a data file, for example data/course.yml on the main branch, you see three kinds of text. VS Code shows each in its own colour:


Explanations (grey in the screenshot): lines that start with #. They explain how the file works and what each field does, and don’t appear on your website. You can delete them if you prefer a shorter file, but they are useful to keep while you are getting to know the template.
Field names (green): the word before the colon, for example title:. They tell the template where each piece of information goes on your website. Never change field names. If you do, the template can’t find that information any more.
Values (blue): the text after the colon, usually between quotation marks. This is what you change. It is the information that appears on your website.

For example, in this line:
title: "Training title"
title is the field name: leave it as it is. "Training title" is the value: replace it with the title of your training.






Note



The colours depend on the colour theme you use in VS Code, so yours may look different from the screenshot. The rule is always the same: lines starting with # are explanations, the word before the colon is the field name, and the text after the colon is the value you change.








Warning



Keep the layout
Data files are very sensitive to layout:

Keep the spaces at the start of each line exactly as they are. They show which information belongs together.
Keep the quotation marks around values.
Lines starting with - are list items. To add an item, copy a whole line and change its value.

If the preview shows an error after you save a data file, check these first. The error message usually names the file and the line.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
Next steps
Now that you know your way around, continue with:

Landing page: describe your training on the landing page.
Training instances: create the website for each time your training is given.
FAIRification: make your training citable and findable.




This User Guide is maintained by the SciLifeLab Training Hub.
Questions, problems or ideas for improving the guide or the template? Open an issue or email us at training@scilifelab.se.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
Before you start
The landing page is the front door of your training. It introduces the training as a whole, and helps visitors decide whether to register, or which training instance to open.
The figure below shows the parts of the landing page, and the names this guide uses for them.
In this chapter, you will learn how to:
Everything in this chapter happens on the main branch, and almost all of it in the four data files in the data folder:
Work as described in Regular workflow: start the preview with python scripts/preview.py, make your changes, save them, and check them in your browser. You don’t have to commit after every change: you can make several changes, and commit and push them together.
If you’re not sure how a data file works, see Data files.
At the end of the chapter, a cheat sheet box sums up which file to open and what to change. It is handy when you come back to the guide later.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.1 Switch off template mode
Your repository starts as a copy of the template, so it still presents itself as the template. You can see this in the yellow Want to use this template? banner at the top of the landing page (see overview image above). Switching off template mode turns your repository into your own training. Do this first:

On the main branch, open data/website.yml.
Find the line:
template: true
Change it to:
template: false
Save the file (Cmd+S (macOS) or Ctrl+S (Windows and Linux))

This changes two things:

The yellow banner disappears from the landing page.
The README, CITATION.cff and .zenodo.json now describe your training, using your data files. While template mode was on, they described the template itself.


Done when: the yellow banner is gone from the preview.


Replace the README
Your repository’s README, the description shown on its main page on GitHub, still describes the template. Replace it with the README for a training:

In the Explorer panel, open the docs folder and then _template-README.md.
Select all text (Cmd+A or Ctrl+A) and copy it.
Open README.md in the main folder of your repository, select all text, and paste, so the copied text replaces it.
Delete the note at the top of the file, between <!-- and -->, and the line starting with > **Template:**.
Fill in the parts marked Write this yourself. The other parts, between <!-- generated:... --> lines, are filled in automatically from your data files.
Save the file.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.2 Change the title and subtitle
The hero is the large dark banner at the top of the landing page. It is the first thing visitors see, and shows the title and subtitle of your training, the logos and the buttons.

Open data/course.yml.
Find the lines:
title: "Training title"
subtitle: "Training subtitle"
Replace the text between the quotation marks with the title and subtitle of your training.
Save the file.

The title is also used as the title of your website in the browser tab, in the README and in the citation of your training.






Tip



Keep the subtitle to one sentence, and start it with an action verb such as Learn, Understand, Explore, Build or Apply. For example:

Learn how to apply open science practices throughout the research lifecycle.

The subtitle is optional: to leave it out, change it to subtitle: "".

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.3 Add or remove logos
The logos in the hero show the organisations behind your training. You can add logos, remove them, or replace them with your own.

Add a logo

Save your logo as an SVG or PNG file.






Tip



Use a white version of your logo, or one made for a dark background, so it stands out against the dark hero.


Copy the file into the img/logos folder: drag it from your computer onto the folder in the Explorer panel in VS Code.
Open data/website.yml and find the hero part:
hero:
  logos:
    - src: "img/logos/SciLifeLab_Logotype_NEG.png"
      alt: "SciLifeLab"
Add your logo at the bottom of the list. Copy the two lines of an existing logo, from - src: to alt:, and paste them below. Then change the values:

src: where the file is, starting with img/logos/, followed by the file name;
alt: the name of the organisation. Screen readers read this out for visitors who can’t see the logo.

For example:
hero:
  logos:
    - src: "img/logos/SciLifeLab_Logotype_NEG.png"
      alt: "SciLifeLab"
    - src: "img/logos/my-organisation.svg"
      alt: "My organisation"
Save the file.

The logos appear in the same order as in the list.






Note



Keep the spaces at the start of each line exactly as in the example: the - src: line of every logo starts at the same position, and alt: lines up with src:.
The file name in src must match the name of your file exactly, including capital letters and the extension (.svg or .png).




Remove a logo

Open data/website.yml and find the hero part.
Delete both lines of the logo you want to remove: the - src: line and the alt: line below it.
Save the file.
Optional: if you no longer need the logo file, delete it from the img/logos folder. In VS Code, right-click the file and choose Delete.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.4 Edit the information cards
The information cards below the hero describe your training. They are created from your data files:







Card
Comes from




Training content
description in data/course.yml


Learning outcomes
learning_outcomes in data/course.yml


Keywords
keywords in data/course.yml


Topics covered
topics in data/course.yml (optional)


Founders
People with the role Founder in data/team.yml


Contributors
People with the role Contributor in data/team.yml



The same information is also used in the README and the citation of your training, and helps people find it in Zenodo and training registries such as TeSS.

Training content

Open data/course.yml and find description:
description: |
  Description of the content of the training.

  Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit...
Replace the example text below description: | with a description of your training. Keep the two spaces at the start of every line. Separate paragraphs with an empty line.

The | after description: lets you write several lines and paragraphs. You can also use simple formatting, such as **bold** or links: [link text](https://example.org).






Tip



Focus on what the training covers. Around ten sentences is usually enough.




Learning outcomes, keywords and topics
These three are lists: each line starting with - is one item.

Open data/course.yml and find learning_outcomes, keywords or topics:
learning_outcomes:
  - "Learning outcome 1"
  - "Learning outcome 2"
  - "Learning outcome 3"
Replace the example text between the quotation marks with your own.
To add an item, copy a whole line, paste it below, and change the text. To remove an item, delete its whole line.

The learning outcomes are numbered automatically on the website.






Tip




Learning outcomes describe what participants will be able to do after the training. For guidance, see the SciLifeLab Training Hub resources on writing learning outcomes.
Keywords: around four or five short terms that describe the main subject areas. They help people find your training.
Topics: short phrases, not full sentences, that give visitors a quick overview of what the training covers.



The Topics covered card is optional. To leave it out, replace the list with an empty one:
topics: []


Founders and contributors
The Founders and Contributors cards list the people in data/team.yml:

Founders started the training, or are responsible for it.
Contributors contributed materials or expertise.

Each person looks like this:
- given_names: "Firstname1"
  family_names: "Lastname1"
  roles:
    - Founder
  affiliation: "Institution or organisation"
  orcid: ""
  citation_author: true

Open data/team.yml.
Fill in the details of each person:

given_names and family_names: first name(s) and surname. Put words like “van der” in the surname.
roles: Founder or Contributor.
affiliation: the organisation the person works for.

To add a person, copy a whole entry, from - given_names: to the last line before the next - given_names:, paste it below, and change the values. To remove a person, delete their whole entry.

Each card is left out when nobody has that role. The other fields, such as orcid, email, course_contact and citation_author, are used for the citation of your training. They are explained in FAIRification and in the comments at the top of data/team.yml.






Important



Every person needs given_names, family_names, roles and affiliation. If one is missing, the preview shows an error that names the person and the missing field.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.5 List your training instances
The All training instances banner near the bottom of the landing page has a button for each training instance. Visitors use it to open the website of the current training, or of an earlier one.
The list comes from data/instances.yml. Each training instance looks like this:
- slug: "2605"
  label: "May 2026"
  status: current
  visible: true
  show_in_hero: true
  instance_url: "./2605/"
  registration_url: "https://example.org/registration"
  sort_key: 202605







Field
What it means




slug
The year and month of the training instance as YYMM, the same as in its branch name. For example, "2605" for the branch release-2605


label
The text on the button, for example "May 2026"


status
current for the training instance that is running now or coming up next; previous for earlier ones


visible
true to show the button in the banner; false to hide it


show_in_hero
Only for the current training instance: whether the hero shows a button to it. See Set up the hero buttons


instance_url
The link to the website of the training instance: "./YYMM/", with the same digits as slug


registration_url
Only for the current training instance: the link to its registration page


sort_key
The year and month as YYYYMM, for example 202605. Used to put the training instances in order









Important




Exactly one training instance has status: current. All others have status: previous.
The current training instance always has visible: true.
Each training instance has its own slug: never use the same one twice.
slug and instance_url use the same four digits.

If one of these rules is broken, the preview shows an error that explains what to fix.



Remove the example training instances
The template’s list contains example training instances, such as 2505 and 2411, that don’t exist in your repository. Their buttons would lead to pages that don’t exist. Start by removing them:

Open data/instances.yml.
Delete the whole entry of each example instance, from - slug: to sort_key:, except the one with slug: "0000".
Save the file.

Keep the 0000 entry for now: it links to the example training instance on the release-0000 branch. You replace it once your first own training instance is ready.


Add a training instance
Each training instance has its own release- branch, with its own website. Adding it to instances.yml puts a button to that website on the landing page.






Note



Creating a release- branch does not add it to this list automatically. First create the branch, as described in Training instances, and then add it here.



Open data/instances.yml.
Copy a complete entry, from - slug: to sort_key:, and paste it at the top of the list, directly under instances:.
Change slug, label, instance_url and sort_key to the new training instance.
If the new training instance is now the current one, see Change the current training instance below.
Save the file.

For example, for a training instance in November 2026:
- slug: "2611"
  label: "November 2026"
  status: current
  visible: true
  show_in_hero: true
  instance_url: "./2611/"
  registration_url: "https://example.org/registration"
  sort_key: 202611






Note



Keep the spaces at the start of each line exactly as in the existing entries: - slug: is indented by two spaces, and the other lines of the entry by four.




Change the current training instance
When a new training instance becomes the current one:

In data/instances.yml, find the training instance that is current now, and change its status and show_in_hero:
status: previous
show_in_hero: false
Find the new current training instance, and set:
status: current
visible: true
show_in_hero: true
Save the file.

For example:
instances:

  - slug: "2611"
    label: "November 2026"
    status: current
    visible: true
    show_in_hero: true
    instance_url: "./2611/"
    registration_url: "https://example.org/registration"
    sort_key: 202611

  - slug: "2605"
    label: "May 2026"
    status: previous
    visible: true
    show_in_hero: false
    instance_url: "./2605/"
    registration_url: ""
    sort_key: 202605


Show or hide an earlier training instance
You may not want to show every earlier training instance on the landing page. To hide one, set its visible to false:
visible: false
To show it again, set it back to true. A hidden training instance stays in the list, and its website stays online: only its button disappears from the banner.






Warning



Never hide the current training instance with visible: false. To remove its button from the hero, use show_in_hero: false instead. See Set up the hero buttons.




Change the text on a button
Change the label of the training instance, for example from "May 2026" to "Spring 2026". This only changes the text visitors see, not where the button leads.


Change the order
The current training instance is always shown first. The earlier ones follow, newest first, sorted by sort_key. You don’t need to put the entries in order yourself, as long as each sort_key is the year and month of its training instance, written as YYYYMM: for example, 202605 for May 2026.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.6 Set up the hero buttons
The hero can show two buttons:

Take me to the current instance opens the website of the current training instance.
Register now opens the registration page of the current training instance.

Both buttons use the training instance with status: current in data/instances.yml. See List your training instances to set which one that is.

Add the registration link

Open data/instances.yml and find the training instance with status: current.
Replace the example link in registration_url with the link to your registration page or form:
registration_url: "https://your-registration-page.example"
Save the file.



Hide the registration button
When registration has closed, or your training doesn’t need registration, empty the link of the current training instance:
registration_url: ""
The Register now button disappears. To show it again, fill in the link again.


Hide the current instance button
When there is no current training instance to point to, for example when your training is self-paced or not given at the moment, set show_in_hero of the current training instance to false:
show_in_hero: false
The button disappears from the hero. The training instance stays in the All training instances banner.


Change the button texts
You can change the text on the buttons, and the heading of the All training instances banner, without changing where they lead:

Open data/website.yml and find the labels part:
labels:
  hero_view_current_label: "Take me to the current instance"
  hero_registration_open_label: "Register now"
  instances_band_title: "All training instances"
Change the text between the quotation marks. For example:
hero_view_current_label: "Go to the latest training"
hero_registration_open_label: "Sign up"
Save the file.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.7 Change the banner image
The All training instances banner shows a decorative image next to the buttons. You can replace it with an image that fits your training.

Copy your image into the img/images folder: drag it from your computer onto the folder in the Explorer panel in VS Code.






Tip



Use a landscape image. The image is cropped automatically to fill the space, so keep the important part near the middle.


Open data/website.yml and find:
instances_band:
  image: "img/images/navet-band.png"
Replace navet-band.png with the file name of your image, for example:
instances_band:
  image: "img/images/my-training-banner.jpg"
Save the file, and check the preview at different widths of your browser window.

To show no image at all, set image: "".






TipIs the important part of your image cut off?





You can choose which part of the image stays visible. This is the only change in this guide in styles.css, the file that controls the look of the website, so make it carefully:

Open styles.css and search for .instances-band__image (Cmd+F or Ctrl+F).
In that block, find:
object-position: center;
Change center to the part you want to keep. For example, center top keeps the top of the image, and 30% center moves the visible part to the left.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.8 Edit the footer
The footer at the bottom of the landing page shows who runs the training, its licence, how the website was built, and a link to your repository on GitHub. All of it is in the footer part of data/website.yml.

Organisation
Change organisation to the name of the organisation, programme or group responsible for your training:
organisation: "SciLifeLab Training Hub"


Licence
The licence tells others how they may reuse your training. The footer shows its name, linked to the page that explains it:
licence:
  name: "CC BY 4.0"
  url: "https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/"






Important



The licence also appears in reuse in data/course.yml, where it’s used for the README and the citation. If you choose another licence, change it in both files, so they say the same, and replace the text in LICENSE.md. See FAIRification for help choosing a licence.




Repository link
The GitHub logo in the footer links to your repository. Replace url with the address of your repository on GitHub:
repository:
  url: "https://github.com/your-organisation/your-repository"
  image: "img/logos/Github_Neg.png"
  alt: "GitHub repository"
You find the address in your browser’s address bar when you open your repository on GitHub, for example https://github.com/SciLifeLab-Training/introduction-to-r.






Important



The repository link is required. The template also uses it to work out the address of your website, for the citation of your training.




Built with
The built_with part credits the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template. You can usually leave it as it is.

title: 7  FAIRification and publishing your course
section: 7.2 Make your materials easy to cite
text:
7.2 Make your materials easy to cite
To make your training easier to cite, you can provide citation information in a CITATION.cff file. This file contains structured information about how your training materials should be cited, including the course title, authors, ORCID identifiers, licence, and links to the course repository and website.

7.2.1 Create the citation file for your course
The SciLifeLab Course Page Template already contains a CITATION.cff file in the root of the repository on the main branch. This file describes the template itself. When you use the template for your own course, replace the contents of CITATION.cff with citation information for your own training materials.

In the main branch, open CITATION.cff.
Delete the existing contents of the file.
Copy and paste the following starter text:

cff-version: 1.2.0
message: "If you use these training materials, please cite them as below."

title: "COURSE TITLE"

authors:
  - family-names: "SURNAME"
    given-names: "GIVEN NAME"
    orcid: "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"

license: CC-BY-4.0

repository-code: "https://github.com/ORGANISATION/REPOSITORY"
url: "https://ORGANISATION.github.io/REPOSITORY/"

references:
  - type: software
    title: "SciLifeLab Course Page Template"
    repository-code: "PERMANENT TEMPLATE REPOSITORY URL"

Replace the placeholder values with information about your course.








Field
What to enter




title
The title of your course or training materials.


family-names
The author’s family name or surname.


given-names
The author’s given name(s).


orcid
The author’s ORCID identifier, if they have one.


license
The licence under which the training materials are made available.


repository-code
The URL of the GitHub repository containing your course materials.


url
The URL of the published course website.









Important



Keep:
cff-version: 1.2.0
unchanged. This is the version of the Citation File Format specification, not the version of your course.




7.2.2 Add multiple authors
Add a separate entry under authors for each person who should be credited as an author of the training materials.
For example:
authors:
  - family-names: "Smith"
    given-names: "Anna"
    orcid: "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"

  - family-names: "Jones"
    given-names: "David"
    orcid: "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"
If an author does not have an ORCID, simply omit the orcid line:
authors:
  - family-names: "Jones"
    given-names: "David"






Tip



ORCID provides researchers with a persistent identifier that distinguishes them from other researchers. If your contributors have ORCID identifiers, include them in CITATION.cff.




7.2.3 Acknowledge this template in your course
The starter file contains the following entry:
references:
  - type: software
    title: "SciLifeLab Course Page Template"
    repository-code: "PERMANENT TEMPLATE REPOSITORY URL"
Keep this entry when adapting CITATION.cff for your course. It acknowledges the SciLifeLab Course Page Template as the resource used to create your course website.


7.2.4 Citation files for individual course instances
How you manage CITATION.cff depends on how you publish your course materials.
If your course is maintained as one continuously updated resource, you can maintain the citation information in the main branch.
If individual course instances are released separately (in this template by adding and publishing branches), their citation information may also differ. For example, different instances may have different contributors.
In this case, update CITATION.cff in the specific course-instance branch before creating the release. This allows the citation metadata for that release to reflect the people and materials associated with that particular course instance.






Tip



Before publishing a course instance, check that CITATION.cff contains the correct title, authors, ORCIDs, licence, repository URL, and course website URL for the materials you are releasing.



Quick reference
 Make your course citable 








To…
File
Edit




Add citation information for your course
CITATION.cff
Replace the template citation metadata with the starter CFF and enter your course information.


Add an author
CITATION.cff
Add another entry under authors.


Add an ORCID
CITATION.cff
Add the author’s ORCID using the orcid field.


Credit an author without an ORCID
CITATION.cff
Include their name and omit the orcid field.


Cite a particular course instance
CITATION.cff in the course-instance branch
Update the citation metadata before creating the release.
